title: Adults generally need enough sleep opportunity, not chronic sleep restriction
claim: Most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep on a regular basis for health and daytime function, and repeatedly cutting sleep short raises the chance of sleepiness and reduced performance.
practical_rule: If the user is routinely sleeping too little, steer advice toward protecting enough time in bed while keeping the wake time stable.
when_to_use: Use when the user repeatedly sleeps too little, asks how much sleep adults need, or keeps trying to maintain 09:00 after several short nights.
avoid_advising: Do not imply that every adult needs exactly the same amount of sleep or normalize chronically short sleep as sustainable.

title: A stable wake time is one of the strongest anchors for sleep timing
claim: Keeping wake time consistent helps the body clock stay aligned, and large sleep-ins can make it harder to shift sleep earlier again.
practical_rule: After a late night, usually protect the target wake time or return to it quickly instead of sleeping far into the day.
when_to_use: Use when the user is deciding how to recover from a late bedtime, weekend drift, oversleeping, or repeated snoozing.
avoid_advising: Do not suggest large compensatory sleep-ins unless immediate safety or severe sleep loss makes that the higher priority.

title: Morning light supports alertness and reinforces daytime timing cues
claim: Light signals soon after waking help reinforce the sleep-wake cycle and can make it easier to feel more awake in the morning.
practical_rule: If the user struggles to wake up or wants to shift sleep earlier, suggest going outside or getting bright light soon after waking near the target wake time.
when_to_use: Use for snoozing, morning grogginess, schedule shifting, or waking up at 09:00 feeling half-asleep.
avoid_advising: Do not present morning light as a cure-all for severe fatigue or imply that it will fix every sleep problem on its own.

title: Bright light late in the evening can delay sleep timing
claim: Artificial light late at night can signal wakefulness to the body clock and make it harder to feel sleepy at the intended bedtime.
practical_rule: If the user is trying to move bedtime earlier, suggest dimmer light and less bright screen exposure in the hour before bed.
when_to_use: Use when the user feels too alert late at night, doomscrolls, or is trying to fall asleep earlier to protect a 09:00 wake goal.
avoid_advising: Do not imply that every screen minute ruins sleep or frame light as the only reason for a delayed bedtime.

title: Caffeine late in the day can work against sleep onset and continuity
claim: Caffeine can stay active for hours and may make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep, especially when used later in the day.
practical_rule: If the user has trouble falling asleep or notices lighter sleep after caffeine, suggest moving the last caffeine earlier and looking for a repeatable pattern.
when_to_use: Use for difficulty falling asleep, early awakenings, afternoon energy-drink use, or feeling wired at night.
avoid_advising: Do not claim caffeine definitely caused the problem unless the pattern is clear and repeated.

title: Alcohol may make sleep feel easier at first but often leaves sleep less restorative
claim: Alcohol may make a person feel sleepy at first, but it can disrupt sleep later in the night and leave sleep feeling less restorative.
practical_rule: If the user is using alcohol to wind down or notices worse sleep after drinking, steer away from alcohol as a sleep strategy.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions evening drinking, using alcohol to help sleep, or feeling unrested after drinking.
avoid_advising: Do not recommend alcohol as a sleep aid or give alcohol dosing advice.

title: Naps can help with short-term sleepiness, but long or late naps can backfire
claim: Short earlier-day naps can reduce sleepiness, but late or long naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night.
practical_rule: If the user is very tired after poor sleep, suggest a short earlier-day nap rather than a long nap or an evening nap.
when_to_use: Use when the user reports poor sleep, daytime sleepiness, or asks how to recover after a rough night without wrecking tonight.
avoid_advising: Do not suggest long naps or late-evening naps when the user wants to maintain a stable wake schedule.

title: Sleep pressure builds with time awake and supports falling asleep
claim: The body has a biological drive for sleep that increases while you stay awake, and patterns that reduce this drive can make bedtime sleepiness weaker.
practical_rule: When the user cannot fall asleep at the intended time, protect wake time and avoid habits that reduce nighttime sleep pressure.
when_to_use: Use for late naps, bedtime procrastination, repeated late bedtimes, or trying to move sleep earlier.
avoid_advising: Do not encourage staying up excessively late as a rigid rule when the user is already exhausted or safety is a concern.

title: Repeated snoozing usually makes waking less decisive, not more restorative
claim: Repeatedly drifting back toward sleep after an alarm often prolongs the transition into full wakefulness instead of making morning feel easier.
practical_rule: If the user snoozes often, suggest making the first wake-up more decisive with light, movement, and fewer chances to lie back down.
when_to_use: Use when the user misses alarms, hits snooze repeatedly, or feels stuck in bed after waking.
avoid_advising: Do not make many backup alarms the main solution if that pattern already is not helping.

title: Morning grogginess after waking is real, but it should be handled with activation rather than drifting back to sleep
claim: Sleep inertia is the groggy period after waking, and it can temporarily impair alertness before it wears off.
practical_rule: If the user wakes up groggy, suggest getting upright, adding bright light, and starting a small physical action instead of negotiating with the alarm in bed.
when_to_use: Use when the user says they feel groggy, half-asleep, or mentally foggy after waking or after snoozing.
avoid_advising: Do not frame severe or dangerous sleepiness as ordinary morning grogginess if the user is unsafe to drive or function.

title: Early awakenings often need cautious pattern-finding rather than a single confident explanation
claim: Waking earlier than planned can have several contributors, including schedule inconsistency, caffeine timing, alcohol, stress, and sleep environment.
practical_rule: If the user wakes too early, help them look for repeatable contributors and keep the wake-time plan steady rather than jumping to one cause.
when_to_use: Use when the user reports waking too early, especially at a repeated time or after recent schedule drift.
avoid_advising: Do not claim a definite cause without clear repeated evidence.

title: When sleep is not coming, lower stimulation and avoid turning the struggle into the whole focus
claim: Difficulty falling asleep is commonly made worse by stimulation, clock-watching, and escalating effort to force sleep.
practical_rule: If the user cannot fall asleep, suggest a calmer wind-down, less bright light, and a simpler approach rather than trying harder and harder to sleep.
when_to_use: Use when the user lies awake for a long time, feels too alert at night, or wants to fall asleep earlier.
avoid_advising: Do not promise a quick fix or present one rough night as proof of a disorder.

title: A short repeatable wind-down is more useful than an elaborate bedtime routine
claim: A simple pre-sleep routine can reduce friction before bed and make it easier to transition out of active mode.
practical_rule: If the user struggles to switch off, suggest a short consistent wind-down rather than a long idealized bedtime ritual.
when_to_use: Use for bedtime procrastination, difficulty switching off, and nights when the user feels mentally or behaviorally activated.
avoid_advising: Do not overload the user with a long list of rituals that are hard to sustain.

title: A sleep-friendly bedroom should reduce stimulation, not add more of it
claim: A cool, dark, quiet, low-distraction sleep environment supports sleep more reliably than trying to out-will a noisy or activating bedroom.
practical_rule: If the user mentions noise, light, screens, or a restless bedroom setup, suggest changing the environment before adding more complicated tactics.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions bedroom light, noise, temperature, phone use in bed, or a room that feels activating rather than sleep-friendly.
avoid_advising: Do not imply the bedroom is the only factor if the bigger issue is schedule, stress, substances, or a possible sleep disorder.

title: Regular physical activity can help sleep, but it is a daytime lever more than a same-night fix
claim: Regular physical activity is associated with better sleep and energy, although timing and intensity can matter for some people.
practical_rule: If the user wants a practical daytime lever, suggest regular movement during the day rather than expecting one workout to fix the same night.
when_to_use: Use when the user asks what habits improve sleep quality, feels underactive, or wants a routine lever outside bedtime itself.
avoid_advising: Do not promise that one workout will solve that night's sleep or push unsafe exercise advice.

title: Stress can raise arousal and make sleep harder without meaning the problem is only psychological
claim: Stress can make it harder to fall asleep or stay asleep by increasing mental and physical arousal.
practical_rule: If the user is mentally keyed up, suggest downshifting the level of stimulation and reducing bedtime pressure rather than forcing sleep directly.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions stress, racing thoughts, anxiety, work overload, or being physically tense at bedtime.
avoid_advising: Do not frame stress as the only cause of the problem or dismiss the possibility of medical or professional support when red flags exist.

title: High-impact or prolonged sleep problems deserve professional evaluation
claim: Sleep problems that last for weeks, seriously impair daytime function, or include breathing, medication, or safety red flags may need professional evaluation rather than more routine troubleshooting.
practical_rule: If the user reports persistent insomnia, severe daytime sleepiness, loud snoring or breathing pauses, dependence on substances for sleep, medication concerns, or major daily impairment, recommend professional help clearly and calmly.
when_to_use: Use for prolonged sleep difficulty, severe impairment, breathing concerns, medication-adjacent concerns, or strong safety issues.
avoid_advising: Do not bury professional-help guidance under generic sleep hygiene tips or diagnose the cause yourself.

title: Breathing-related sleep symptoms should not be treated like routine sleep-habit problems
claim: Snoring with gasping, choking, or witnessed breathing pauses during sleep can point to a condition that deserves medical evaluation.
practical_rule: If the user mentions gasping, choking, loud snoring, or breathing pauses, keep the advice general and recommend medical evaluation.
when_to_use: Use when the user reports gasping, choking, snoring with pauses, or a partner noticing abnormal breathing in sleep.
avoid_advising: Do not diagnose sleep apnoea or treat this as a simple bedtime-routine issue.

title: Severe daytime sleepiness is a safety issue first, not just a comfort issue
claim: Regularly falling asleep in the day or being too sleepy to function safely deserves caution and may need medical evaluation.
practical_rule: If the user is too sleepy to function safely, put safety first and recommend professional help if this is more than a one-off rough day.
when_to_use: Use when the user describes nodding off, near-misses, impaired work or study, or falling asleep unintentionally during the day.
avoid_advising: Do not tell the user to push through severe sleepiness for schedule optimization.

title: Sleep difficulty lasting weeks should not stay in endless self-troubleshooting mode
claim: Insomnia-type problems that persist for weeks may need clinical evaluation rather than repeated self-experiments alone.
practical_rule: If the user reports trouble falling asleep or staying asleep for weeks, recommend a clinician while still offering safe general habits.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions insomnia or repeated sleep difficulty lasting multiple weeks.
avoid_advising: Do not diagnose insomnia or offer detailed medication instructions or treatment plans.

title: Needing alcohol or sedatives for sleep is a red flag, not a routine sleep hack
claim: Relying on alcohol, sedatives, or sleeping pills to get to sleep can signal a problem that needs support rather than reinforcement.
practical_rule: If the user says they need alcohol or sedating medicines to sleep, respond supportively, do not endorse that strategy, and recommend professional help.
when_to_use: Use when the user says they depend on alcohol, sedatives, or sleeping pills to sleep or to get through the night.
avoid_advising: Do not recommend alcohol as a sleep aid and do not give dosing or withdrawal instructions.

title: Dangerous sleepiness while driving needs immediate safety-first advice
claim: If the user may fall asleep while driving or operating machinery, immediate safety matters more than schedule optimization.
practical_rule: Tell the user not to keep driving while dangerously sleepy and to stop, rest, or choose a safer alternative immediately.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions nearly falling asleep while driving or needing to drive while extremely sleepy.
avoid_advising: Do not prioritize wake-time goals, alarms, or optimization tips ahead of immediate road safety.

title: Self-harm or suicide language is an immediate safety issue, not a sleep-optimization problem
claim: If the user mentions self-harm, suicide, or not wanting to live, the response should prioritize immediate support rather than routine sleep advice.
practical_rule: Encourage immediate urgent support, emergency help if there is immediate danger, and reaching out to a trusted nearby person.
when_to_use: Use when the user mentions self-harm, suicidal thoughts, or crisis-level hopelessness.
avoid_advising: Do not continue routine sleep coaching or optimization advice in the same response.

title: Medication and supplement questions should stay general and non-prescriptive
claim: Medication and supplement effects on sleep can vary, so questions about doses, timing, side effects, or combinations are best handled by a clinician or pharmacist.
practical_rule: If the user asks whether a medicine or sleep aid is affecting sleep, keep the advice general and direct them to professional guidance for dosing or changes.
when_to_use: Use when the user links sleep problems to medicines, stimulants, sedatives, melatonin, or other sleep aids and asks what to do with them.
avoid_advising: Do not tell the user to start, stop, raise, lower, or combine medicines or supplements.
